provenance.notes: Replaces the retired break-even pack. The scheme, its four bands, its rates and its four stipulations are invented for this pack; nothing here is a textbook relationship a candidate could bring with them, which is what §5.10 requires and what the retired pack could not satisfy.

repairs.reason: q2 could be narrowed using q3. q3’s answer establishes that a band re-rates the whole year’s quantity rather than the units above the band’s lower limit, and q2’s smallest option was the only one consistent with re-rating the marginal units alone — so knowing the scheme is retrospective eliminated it without any arithmetic. Repairing that moved the same fault onto q1, whose own marginal-only option could then be eliminated on the scale q2’s remaining options reveal; q1 is repaired in the same way and for the same reason.

changed.gam-ba-sr-001-q2: Option set replaced. All four options are now consistent with whole-quantity re-rating and differ only in which rate is applied to which year total, so q3’s answer separates none of them. The stem, the key, the computation and the learning objective are unchanged.
changed.gam-ba-sr-001-q1: Moved from 950 units to 1,600, and its marginal-only distractor retired. Repairing q2 by dropping its one small option tightened the visible spread of its remaining three, which sharpened rather than removed the signal that this scheme pays in thousands — and that signal was enough to eliminate q1’s 210-euro option on scale alone. A question one band up, whose four options all sit in the same order of magnitude, cannot be attacked that way. The retrospective-rule trap survives in a form that scale cannot pick off: applying the rate to the band’s lower limit instead of to the year’s total.

repairs.unchanged: q1, q3, q4 and q5 keep their content; q3 was the leak source and its own content is sound.

retiredQuestions.stem: A buyer expects to need 1,800 units over the next fourteen months and can place the orders whenever it suits. According to the scheme, which arrangement earns the larger rebate?
retiredQuestions.reason: Retired as non-discriminating, not as incorrect. Two independent adjudication rounds agreed with its key. Both ablation halves answered it with no source at all — Claude Sonnet 5 on 7 September, Claude Opus 5 on 8 September at high confidence — and the Opus round rated it decisively leaked by q1 and q2: q2 shows numerically that twenty units inside one calendar year move the rebate by roughly 1,600 euros, which eliminates the "timing does not matter" option outright, and q1 shows the per-unit rate rising with the year’s total, which is the rest of the argument. An item answerable without the pack and readable off its siblings adds nothing. Reworking it as a computation was rejected: every numeric option in this pack is a unit count times a band rate, so a further numeric item would expose one more point on the rate ladder the Opus round showed is already recoverable across siblings. The id is reserved and never reused.

provenance.retiredBecause: Superseded by the production candidate set of 8-9 September 2026, and retired on promotion rather than deleted. No key in this pack is wrong: two independent rounds agreed with every one of them, and it carries no ambiguity, outside-knowledge or §5.10 finding. It is retired because of how it was built. It predates the independent-source architecture, and under the same adjudicator that cleared the candidate set every one of the pilot’s sixteen questions carried a narrowing sibling coupling, against seven of nineteen in the set replacing it. Keeping both active would ship two authoring standards at once. Its questions, provenance and adjudication history are kept in full as the record of how the architecture was arrived at; the ids are reserved and never reused.

blocks.text: A wholesaler sells a single product at a list price of 60 euros per unit and operates what it calls a step rebate. At the end of each calendar year the wholesaler totals the units a buyer has bought, places that total in a band, and pays back a percentage of what the buyer spent. The scheme is not a discount at the point of sale: the buyer pays the list price on every order and receives the rebate afterwards.

items: The rebate is retrospective: the band’s rate applies to every unit bought in the year, and not only to the units above the band’s lower limit.
Every unit bought in the year counts towards the band, whatever price was actually paid for it.
The rebate is calculated on the list price of the units, and never on a price that a separate discount has already reduced.
Units returned are taken out of the year’s total on the day they are returned.
A year’s purchases do not carry over. Each calendar year is banded on its own.

blocks.text: If a return takes the year’s total below the lower limit of a band that has already been credited, the whole of the rebate credited under that band is recovered from the buyer, and the rebate is worked out again at the band the reduced total now falls in. A return that leaves the total inside the same band changes the amount of the rebate but not the rate at which it is worked out.

questions.stem: A buyer’s purchases for the calendar year come to 1,600 units. What rebate is due?

supportSpans.quote: The rebate is retrospective: the band’s rate applies to every unit bought in the year, and not only to the units above the band’s lower limit.
a list price of 60 euros per unit

questions.explanation: 1,600 units falls in the top band, where the rate is 11 per cent. The rate applies to every unit bought in the year, and the rebate is worked out on the list price of 60 euros: 11 per cent of 1,600 × 60 euros, which is 11 per cent of 96,000 euros.

a.reason: This uses the 4 per cent of the 400-to-899 band. The year’s total is 1,600, which is past two further boundaries, and it is the band the total falls in that fixes the rate.

b.reason: This uses the 7 per cent of the 900-to-1499 band. 1,600 is above 1,499, so the year falls in the band above it.

c.reason: This applies the rate to the band’s lower limit of 1,500 rather than to the year’s total. The scheme is retrospective: the rate applies to every unit bought in the year, so all 1,600 count.

hints.text: Place the year’s total in the table of bands before doing any arithmetic.
The rate is a percentage of what the buyer spent, not of the number of units.
Ask how many of the 1,600 units the rate applies to — the list says.

questions.stem: A buyer has bought 880 units and the calendar year is almost over. One further order would take the year’s total to 900. By how much would the year’s rebate increase?

supportSpans.quote: The rebate is retrospective: the band’s rate applies to every unit bought in the year, and not only to the units above the band’s lower limit.

questions.explanation: At 880 units the year sits in the 400-to-899 band, so the rebate is 4 per cent of 880 units at the 60-euro list price: 2,112 euros. The further order takes the total to 900, which falls in the next band at 7 per cent, and that rate applies to every unit bought in the year, not only to the twenty that crossed the line: 7 per cent of 900 units at 60 euros is 3,780 euros. The increase is the difference between the two, 3,780 − 2,112.

a.reason: This works both rebates on 880 units, so the twenty units that carry the year into the higher band earn nothing themselves. They are bought within the year and count like any others.

b.reason: This works both rebates on 900 units. The rebate the buyer already stands to receive is the one due on the year as it is now — 880 units — and it is that figure the increase is measured from.

d.reason: This is the whole rebate the year would earn at 900 units, not the increase. The buyer was already owed a rebate at 880 units, and the question asks by how much the figure moves.

hints.text: Work out the rebate the year earns as it stands, and then the rebate it would earn after the order.
Check which band each of the two totals falls in before choosing a rate.
The higher rate applies to every unit bought in the year, not only to the ones above the band’s lower limit.

questions.stem: Two buyers have each been credited with a rebate, one on a year’s total of 420 units and the other on 600. Before the year ends each of them returns 40 units. According to the scheme, how do the two returns differ in their effect?

options.text: Neither rebate is withdrawn, because the band was fixed when the total passed its lower limit.
Both rebates are withdrawn, and neither buyer is due anything.
The first buyer’s rebate is withdrawn and nothing is due in its place; the second’s is not withdrawn.
The second buyer’s rebate is withdrawn and nothing is due in its place; the first’s is not.

supportSpans.quote: Units returned are taken out of the year’s total on the day they are returned.
the whole of the rebate credited under that band is recovered from the buyer

questions.explanation: Both returns come out of the year’s total. The first buyer falls to 380, below the lowest threshold the scheme sets, so the rebate credited is withdrawn and the reduced total earns none at all. The second falls to 560, still inside the band that was credited, so that rebate stands and only its amount changes.

a.reason: The scheme says the opposite: returned units come out of the year’s total on the day they are returned, so a band once reached is not held.

b.reason: Withdrawal follows only from a return that takes the total below the lower limit of the band already credited. The second buyer stays well inside it.

d.reason: This has the two buyers the wrong way round. It is the smaller total that falls through the scheme’s lowest threshold; the larger one has room to spare.

hints.text: Work out each buyer’s total after the return before looking at what the scheme does about it.
Then ask, for each, whether the reduced total still reaches the band it was credited under.
One of the two falls below the point at which the scheme pays anything at all.

questions.stem: A buyer negotiates a one-off discount off the list price on an order of 200 units, and ends the calendar year with 620 units in total. According to the scheme, does the discounted order count towards the band, and what is its rebate worked out on?

options.text: It counts towards the band, and its rebate is worked out on the price the buyer actually paid.
It counts towards the band, and its rebate is worked out on the list price.
It does not count towards the band, and earns no rebate.
It counts towards the band, but earns no rebate, since a reduction has already been given on it.

supportSpans.quote: Every unit bought in the year counts towards the band, whatever price was actually paid for it.
never on a price that a separate discount has already reduced

questions.explanation: The scheme separates the two questions and answers them differently. What counts towards the band is units, whatever they cost, so all 200 count. What the rebate is worked out on is the list price, never a price a separate discount has already reduced — so the negotiated reduction lowers what the buyer pays and leaves the rebate untouched.

a.reason: The scheme rules this out in terms: the rebate is never worked out on a price a separate discount has already reduced.

c.reason: Every unit bought in the year counts towards the band whatever was paid for it, so a discounted order is not outside the scheme.

d.reason: Nothing in the scheme withholds the rebate from discounted units. It fixes the value the rebate is worked out on, which is a different matter from withholding it.

hints.text: There are two separate questions here; the scheme answers them in two separate places.
One of the conditions says what counts towards the band. Another says what the rebate is worked out on.
They do not give the same answer, and that is the point of the question.
